title: Battery swollen, leaking or smells
h1: Why is my car battery swollen, leaking or smelly?
metaDesc: Car battery swollen, cracked, leaking or smelling like rotten eggs? Why it's dangerous, what not to do, and what usually causes it.
intro: This guide is about the regular 12-volt battery under the hood or in the trunk. A swollen, leaking or smelly battery can give off a gas that explodes and contains acid that burns. Find out what to do and what likely caused it.
safety: Don't jump-start or charge a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, very hot or smells like rotten eggs.
Keep sparks, flames and cigarettes away from the battery. It can give off a gas that explodes.
If battery acid gets in your eyes, rinse them with clean water for at least 15 minutes and get medical help right away.
If the battery is hissing, smoking or boiling, get everyone away from the car. Call 911 if there's smoke or fire.

q_what.q: What do you see or smell?

opts.a: The battery is hissing, smoking, boiling or too hot to touch
The battery case is swollen, bulging or cracked
Crusty buildup, or something wet, on or around the battery

q_swollen.q: Did any of these happen recently?

opts.a: It was jump-started or charged, or the battery light was on
It sat dead in freezing weather, or it's old or has been through hot summers

q_wet.help: Battery terminals are the two metal posts where the cables clamp on.

opts.a: Dry, crusty white, green or blue buildup on the terminals only
Liquid on the battery case, or a wet spot under the battery

q_smell.q: When do you notice the smell?

opts.a: Right after a jump-start, or while a battery charger is connected
While driving, along with the battery light or very bright or flickering lights
From the exhaust, mostly when speeding up

result.title: The battery may be overheating. Get away from it
result.now: Turn off the engine if it's running, get everyone out and stay well away from the car. If there's smoke or fire, call 911. Don't touch the battery or the cables.
if: If a charger is connected and you can safely reach the wall plug, unplug the charger from the wall. Don't touch the clamps on the battery.
Once the battery has cooled down for a long time and nothing is smoking, have it replaced by a battery service or a mechanic. Have the charging system checked too.
result.why: A battery that hisses or boils is breaking down inside, usually from too much charging current. It can give off a gas that explodes and spray acid.

causes.name: Overcharging from the car's charging system
causes.clues: The battery light was on, or the lights were very bright.

causes.name: Battery charger left on or set wrong
causes.clues: A charger was connected.

causes.name: Internal short in the battery
causes.clues: The battery is old, or it happened suddenly.

result.title: The battery may have been overcharged
result.now: Don't drive, jump-start or charge it. Have the battery replaced where the car is, by a mobile battery service or a mechanic, or have the car towed. Ask them to test the charging system too.
if: If the battery light was on while driving, the alternator may be overcharging. A new battery could swell too unless that's fixed.
If you smell rotten eggs or see the battery hissing, get away from the car.
result.why: Too much charging current makes the battery heat up and give off gas, which can make the case swell. The gas can explode if a spark reaches it.

causes.name: Alternator overcharging
causes.clues: The battery light was on, or the headlights were extra bright.

causes.name: Charger left on too long or set wrong
causes.clues: A charger was used recently.

causes.name: Jump-start done wrong
causes.clues: It swelled right after a jump.

you: Note whether the battery light came on recently.

result.title: A swollen battery is damaged inside and must be replaced
result.now: Don't drive, jump-start or charge it. Have the battery replaced where the car is, by a mobile battery service or a mechanic, or have the car towed.
if: If you see acid leaking, don't touch it with bare hands.
If the battery froze, don't try to charge it. A frozen battery can burst.
result.why: Batteries can swell from heat, age, freezing while run down, or overcharging. The case swelling means the inside is damaged. It can leak acid or give off gas that can explode.

causes.name: Old battery worn out by heat
causes.clues: More than a few years old, or lots of hot summers.

causes.name: Froze while run down
causes.clues: The car sat dead in freezing weather.

causes.name: Overcharging
causes.clues: The battery light was on recently.

you: Look at the battery label for its age.

result.title: Corrosion on the terminals is common and often easy to clean
result.now: Wear gloves and eye protection. With the engine off, look at how bad it is. Light buildup can be cleaned with a battery brush and a mix of baking soda and water. Remove the negative (black, minus) cable first and put it back last.
if: If the battery case is cracked, wet or swollen, don't clean it. Have the battery replaced.
If the buildup comes back quickly, have the battery and charging system tested.
If you're not comfortable, a shop can clean the terminals quickly.
result.why: Batteries give off small amounts of acid vapor that react with the metal terminals. The crusty buildup can block power and cause slow or no starting.

causes.name: Normal battery venting over time
causes.clues: Light buildup on an older battery.

causes.name: Overcharging
causes.clues: Heavy buildup that comes back fast.

causes.name: Small leak at a terminal seal
causes.clues: Buildup on one post only, with damp spots.

you: Look at both terminals and the cable ends.
Check whether the cables are tight.

result.title: The battery may be leaking acid
result.now: Don't touch the wet spots with bare hands. Don't drive, jump-start or charge it. Have the battery replaced where the car is, by a mobile battery service or a mechanic, or have the car towed.
if: If acid gets on your skin, wash it off with lots of water. If it burns or hurts, get medical help.
If the wet spot is somewhere else, like under the engine or near a wheel, it may be another fluid. See our fluid leak guide.
result.why: A cracked or overfilled battery can leak acid. Acid eats through metal and wiring and burns skin and eyes. A cracked battery can also fail without warning.

causes.name: Cracked battery case
causes.clues: You can see a crack or bulge.

causes.name: Overcharging
causes.clues: Liquid around the vent caps.

causes.name: Battery tipped or damaged
causes.clues: It was recently moved or the car was hit.

shop: Battery tray and cable inspection for acid damage

result.title: The battery is overheating while being charged
result.now: Stop charging. Unplug the charger from the wall first, if you can reach it safely, and wait for the battery to cool before touching anything. Open the hood and let it air out, and keep sparks and flames away.
if: If the battery is swollen, hissing or leaking, don't charge or jump it again. Have it replaced.
If it was a jump-start, disconnect the cables in the reverse order once the smell has cleared.
result.why: A rotten egg smell during charging means the battery is overheating and giving off gas. This happens when the charging current is too high or the battery is damaged inside.

causes.name: Charger set too high or left on too long
causes.clues: A manual charger was used.

causes.name: Damaged or worn-out battery
causes.clues: The battery is old or wouldn't hold a charge.

causes.name: Cables connected wrong
causes.clues: Sparks or heat when connecting.

result.title: The charging system may be overcharging the battery
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Open the hood to let it air out, and keep sparks away. Have it towed or have a mechanic come to you.
if: If the battery is hissing or smoking, get away from the car and call 911 if there's smoke or fire.
result.why: The alternator's voltage regulator controls how much charge goes into the battery. If it fails, it can push too much, which overheats the battery and makes it give off a rotten egg smell.

causes.name: Failed voltage regulator or alternator
causes.clues: The battery light is on, or lights are very bright or flickering.

causes.name: Damaged battery
causes.clues: The battery is old or swollen.

result.title: A rotten egg smell from the exhaust is usually the catalytic converter, not the battery
result.now: Book a check when convenient. See our rotten egg smell guide for more.
if: If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
If you feel dizzy or get a headache inside the car, open the windows, pull over and get out.
result.why: The exhaust system turns sulfur from fuel into odorless gas. When it isn't working right, you can smell rotten eggs from the tailpipe.

causes.name: Catalytic converter problem
causes.clues: The smell is strongest when speeding up.

causes.name: Engine running rich
causes.clues: The check engine light is on.

you: Note when the smell is strongest.

result.title: Treat a damaged-looking battery with care
result.now: Don't jump-start or charge it until it's checked. With the engine off, look at the battery without touching it. Have it tested within a few days, or sooner if it gets worse.
if: If it's swollen, cracked, leaking, hissing or very hot, don't drive or charge it. Have it replaced where it is.
If you smell rotten eggs near the battery, keep sparks away and let it air out.
result.why: A battery that looks or smells wrong may be damaged. A quick test at a shop or parts store can tell if it's safe to keep using.

causes.name: Worn-out battery
causes.clues: The battery is older than a few years.

causes.name: Charging system problem
causes.clues: The battery light was on.

you: Look at the battery from a safe distance.
